lesson.title: Checking the Fine Print: When Can You Trust the Bell Curve?
lesson.summary: The Central Limit Theorem only kicks in when three conditions are met: randomness, independence, and a large enough sample. This chapter shows how to check each one.
lesson.body:
The Central Limit Theorem promises that the sampling distribution of a statistic like p-hat or x-bar becomes approximately normal as the sample size grows, no matter what the population looks like. That promise is powerful, but it is not unconditional. Before you are allowed to treat a sampling distribution as normal and use normal based methods on it, you have to check that three practical conditions are reasonably satisfied. Skipping this check is one of the most common ways students, and researchers, misuse statistics.

The first condition is randomness. The data must come from a random sample or a randomized experiment. This is not really about the shape of the sampling distribution, it is about whether the sampling distribution formulas for the mean and standard deviation even apply. If people chose themselves into your sample, or you asked only your friends, the resulting sample statistic may be systematically biased in a way that no amount of normal theory can fix.

The second condition is independence. Individual observations must not influence each other. This is automatic in most randomized experiments, but when you are sampling without replacement from a finite population, technically each draw changes the probabilities slightly for the next one. Statisticians handle this with the 10% condition: as long as your sample size n is no more than 10% of the population size N, the dependence between observations is small enough to ignore safely.

The third condition is that the sample size is large enough for the normal approximation to be trustworthy. For a sample proportion, this is checked with the success failure condition: both n times p and n times (1 minus p) must be at least 10, using p-hat in place of p when p is unknown. For a sample mean, the rule of thumb is n of at least 30, unless the population itself is already known to be approximately normal, in which case even a small sample works fine. This condition exists because the CLT is technically a limiting result, exactly true only as n approaches infinity. For small samples from skewed populations, the actual sampling distribution can look quite different from a normal curve, and these numeric thresholds are the field's practical compromise for deciding when "close enough" has been reached.

Suppose a school district wants to estimate what proportion of its 3,000 AP Statistics students own a graphing calculator, based on a random sample of 150 students, of whom 86%, or p-hat equals 0.86, reported owning one. Check the conditions. Randomness: the problem states the sample was randomly selected, so this condition is satisfied. Independence: 10% of 3,000 is 300, and the sample size of 150 is less than 300, so the 10% condition is satisfied. Success failure: n times p-hat equals 150 times 0.86, which is 129, and n times (1 minus p-hat) equals 150 times 0.14, which is 21. Both values are well above 10, so the success failure condition is satisfied. All three conditions hold, so it is reasonable to treat the sampling distribution of p-hat here as approximately normal, which is exactly what lets us use the normal approximation methods in the next section.
